lessons.title: Qualifying an application with STAMPED
lessons.keyPoints:
Most wrong orders come from missing application details, not from the wrong brand.
STAMPED is a checklist for every quote: Size, Temperature, Application, Media, Pressure, Ends (connections), Delivery.
Media drives material choice: ask what the process fluid is, and whether it is corrosive, abrasive, viscous or likely to clog.
Ask for normal and maximum operating pressure and temperature, not just one number.
Ends means the process connection: NPT size, flange class, tri-clamp for sanitary, and so on.
Ask whether the area is hazardous (for example Class I Div 1 or Div 2), since it changes which electronics you can quote.
Ask about special requirements: oxygen-service cleaning, NACE MR0175 for sour service, 3-A sanitary, or calibration certificates.
Always ask what the customer is replacing and why it failed. The failure tells you what to fix.

quiz.q: In STAMPED, what does the "E" stand for?
quiz.why: E is Ends: the process connection, like NPT size, flange class or tri-clamp.

quiz.q: A customer says a gauge "keeps failing." What's the most useful first question?
options: What's the process media, and how did the old one fail?
quiz.why: The media and the failure mode (leaking, clogged, needle shaking) point to the right fix.

quiz.q: Why ask for both normal and maximum operating pressure?
options: To size the range so normal pressure sits mid-scale and spikes don't damage the instrument
quiz.why: Normal pressure sets where the reading sits; maximum pressure makes sure the instrument survives upsets.

quiz.q: A customer's instrument goes in a Class I Div 1 area. What does that tell you?
options: It's a hazardous location, so electronics need the right approvals (for example explosion-proof or intrinsically safe)
quiz.why: Class I Div 1 is a hazardous-location classification for flammable gases or vapors.

lessons.title: Speaking each industry's language
lessons.keyPoints:
Chemical: corrosive media and exotic materials (Hastelloy, Monel, PTFE). Diaphragm seals are common.
Oil & gas: hazardous areas, high pressures, and NACE MR0175 materials for sour (H2S) service.
Water & wastewater: magnetic flowmeters, level and pressure everywhere. Potable water parts may need NSF/ANSI 61.
Food & beverage: sanitary design, 3-A, tri-clamp connections, and equipment that survives washdown and CIP (clean-in-place).
Pharmaceutical: sanitary design plus documentation. Expect calibration certificates, material certs and validation paperwork.
Oxygen service: parts must be cleaned for oxygen service to remove oils and hydrocarbons, which can ignite in oxygen.

quiz.q: A food plant asks for a pressure gauge on a product line. What should you expect to quote?
options: A brass gauge with NPT threads
A sanitary gauge or seal with a tri-clamp connection, suitable for washdown
quiz.why: Food & beverage lines need sanitary designs and tri-clamp connections that can be cleaned.

quiz.q: What does NACE MR0175 relate to?
options: Materials for sour service containing H2S in oil & gas
quiz.why: NACE MR0175 covers materials that resist cracking in H2S (sour) environments.

quiz.q: Why do instruments for oxygen service need special cleaning?
options: Oils and hydrocarbons can ignite in high-concentration oxygen
quiz.why: Hydrocarbon contamination is a fire risk in oxygen, so wetted parts are cleaned to remove it.

quiz.q: A pharmaceutical customer will most often ask for which extra item?
options: Documentation such as calibration and material certificates
quiz.why: Pharma plants validate their equipment, so paperwork is part of the sale.

lessons.title: How gauges work and how to pick the range
lessons.keyPoints:
Most mechanical pressure gauges use a Bourdon tube: a curved tube that straightens slightly as pressure rises and moves the pointer through a gear movement.
Pick a range so normal operating pressure sits in the middle of the dial. A common rule is a range about twice the normal operating pressure.
ASME B40.100 is the standard for pressure gauges in the U.S.
Accuracy is given as a percent of span. Grade 2A is ±0.5% of span; Grade 1A is ±1%.
Common dial sizes are 2.5, 4 and 4.5 inches. Bigger dials are easier to read from a distance.
Wetted parts (the tube and socket) must suit the media: brass for air and water, 316 stainless steel for most process fluids.
Connections are usually 1/4" or 1/2" NPT, bottom or back (center back or lower back) mount.

quiz.q: A line normally runs at 100 psi. Which gauge range is the best fit?
quiz.why: 0–200 puts 100 psi mid-scale, where gauges are most accurate and last longest.

quiz.q: What does a Bourdon tube do?
options: Converts pressure to a 4-20 mA signal
Straightens slightly under pressure to move the pointer
Seals the gauge from corrosive media
quiz.why: The tube flexes with pressure, and that motion drives the pointer through the movement.

quiz.q: A Grade 2A gauge on a 0–200 psi range is accurate to about:
quiz.why: Grade 2A is ±0.5% of span: 0.5% of 200 psi is ±1 psi.

quiz.q: For a mildly corrosive process fluid, which wetted material is the usual default?
quiz.why: 316 SS handles most process fluids. Brass is for air, water and other non-corrosive service.

lessons.title: Protecting gauges in tough service
lessons.keyPoints:
Vibration and pulsation are the top reasons gauges fail early. A shaking needle is the clue.
Liquid filling (glycerin or silicone) dampens vibration and pulsation and keeps the movement lubricated.
A snubber or restrictor in the connection smooths out pressure spikes, like those from pumps or fast-closing valves.
A diaphragm seal isolates the gauge from media that is corrosive, viscous, crystallizing, very hot, or sanitary.
On steam, use a siphon (pigtail) so condensate shields the gauge from high temperature.
If a gauge pegs past full scale, it's under-ranged. Re-size the range or add overpressure protection.

quiz.q: A gauge on a pump discharge has a needle that won't stop shaking. What's the first fix to suggest?
options: A liquid-filled gauge, and a snubber if there are spikes
quiz.why: Liquid fill dampens vibration and pulsation; a snubber handles pressure spikes.

quiz.q: When would you recommend a diaphragm seal?
options: When the dial is hard to read
When the media is corrosive, viscous, clogging or sanitary
When the customer wants a cheaper gauge
quiz.why: A seal keeps difficult media out of the Bourdon tube.

quiz.q: What is a siphon (pigtail) used for?
options: Protecting a gauge from steam temperature
quiz.why: Condensate trapped in the siphon keeps live steam from reaching the gauge.

quiz.q: A customer's gauges keep pegging past full scale. What does that suggest?
options: The case is the wrong material
The range is too low for the actual pressure
quiz.why: Pegging means pressure exceeds the range. Re-size the range or add overpressure protection.

lessons.title: Transmitter basics: types, signals and uses
lessons.keyPoints:
A transmitter turns pressure into a signal a control system can read. A gauge only shows it locally.
Gauge pressure is measured against the atmosphere; absolute pressure against a perfect vacuum.
Differential pressure (DP) transmitters have two ports and measure the difference between them. They're used for flow (with an orifice plate), level, and filter monitoring.
4-20 mA is the standard analog signal. 4 mA is the bottom of the range, so a reading of 0 mA means a broken wire or fault.
HART adds a digital signal on top of 4-20 mA for setup and diagnostics.
Turndown is how far the range can be adjusted down from the maximum. More turndown lets one model cover more applications.
In hazardous areas, transmitters need approvals such as explosion-proof or intrinsically safe.

quiz.q: Why does the 4-20 mA signal start at 4 mA instead of 0?
options: So 0 mA can signal a broken wire or fault
quiz.why: A live zero at 4 mA means a dead signal (0 mA) is clearly a fault, not a zero reading.

quiz.q: Which transmitter type is used with an orifice plate to measure flow?
quiz.why: The orifice creates a pressure drop, and the DP transmitter measures it to infer flow.

quiz.q: What is HART?
options: A digital signal on top of 4-20 mA for setup and diagnostics
quiz.why: HART rides on the analog loop, so you get both the 4-20 mA value and digital data.

quiz.q: A customer needs to measure vacuum independent of weather and altitude changes. Which reference fits?
quiz.why: Absolute pressure is referenced to a perfect vacuum, so atmospheric changes don't affect it.

lessons.title: RTDs, thermocouples and thermowells
lessons.keyPoints:
An RTD changes resistance with temperature. The most common type, Pt100, reads 100 ohms at 0 °C.
RTDs are more accurate and stable over time. They're typically used below about 600 °C.
A thermocouple joins two different metals and produces a small voltage that changes with temperature.
Thermocouples cover higher temperatures, respond faster, and are rugged and lower cost, but are less accurate than RTDs. Type K is the most common general-purpose type.
A thermowell is a closed tube that protects the sensor from the process and lets you remove the sensor without shutting down or draining the line.
In fast-moving fluids, thermowells need a wake frequency calculation (ASME PTC 19.3 TW) to make sure they won't vibrate and break.
A temperature transmitter converts the sensor signal to 4-20 mA for long wire runs.

quiz.q: A customer needs the most accurate, stable reading at 150 °C. Which sensor fits best?
quiz.why: RTDs are the more accurate and stable choice in their temperature range.

quiz.q: A furnace runs at 1,000 °C. Which sensor is the typical choice?
quiz.why: Thermocouples cover much higher temperatures than standard RTDs.

quiz.q: What's the main job of a thermowell?
options: Protect the sensor and allow removal without shutting down the process
quiz.why: The well holds the process pressure, so the sensor can be pulled out while the line runs.

quiz.q: When is a wake frequency calculation needed?
options: When a thermowell sits in fast-flowing fluid that could make it vibrate
quiz.why: Flow past a thermowell sheds vortices; the calculation checks it won't resonate and fail.

lessons.title: Matching the flowmeter to the fluid
lessons.keyPoints:
Start with the fluid: liquid, gas or steam? Clean or dirty? Conductive or not?
Magnetic (mag) meters work only on conductive liquids like water, wastewater and slurries. They have no moving parts and almost no pressure drop. They won't work on oil, gas or deionized water.
Coriolis meters measure mass flow directly, plus density. They're very accurate and work on most liquids and gases, but cost more, especially in large sizes.
Vortex meters handle liquids, gases and steam. They're a common pick for steam.
Differential pressure (DP) flow uses a restriction like an orifice plate and a DP transmitter. It's well understood and works on almost anything, but causes a permanent pressure loss.
Clamp-on ultrasonic meters mount outside the pipe, so they install without cutting the line or shutting down.
Always ask for the flow range (minimum, normal, maximum), pipe size, and required accuracy.

quiz.q: A customer wants to meter diesel fuel. Which meter will NOT work?
quiz.why: Mag meters need a conductive liquid. Diesel and other hydrocarbons aren't conductive.

quiz.q: Which meter measures mass flow directly and also gives density?
quiz.why: Coriolis meters sense mass flow directly from tube vibration and report density too.

quiz.q: A plant can't shut down a line to install a meter. What's a good option to suggest?
quiz.why: Clamp-on ultrasonic mounts on the outside of the pipe, with no cutting or shutdown.

quiz.q: A customer needs to measure saturated steam flow. Which meter is a common choice?
quiz.why: Vortex meters are widely used on steam and handle the temperature well.

lessons.title: Continuous and point level
lessons.keyPoints:
Continuous level gives a reading all the time. Point level switches only signal at one spot, like a high or low alarm.
Non-contact radar works on most liquids and is largely unaffected by temperature, pressure and vapor.
Guided wave radar sends the signal down a probe. It handles foam, vapor, and the interface between two liquids.
Ultrasonic is non-contact and lower cost, but foam, heavy vapor and temperature swings can throw it off.
Hydrostatic (DP) level reads the pressure of the liquid column. If the liquid's density changes, the reading changes.
Point level options include float switches and vibrating fork switches for high and low alarms or pump control.

quiz.q: A tank has heavy foam and vapor. Which is usually more reliable than ultrasonic?
quiz.why: Guided wave radar follows a probe and handles foam and vapor better than ultrasonic.

quiz.q: What's the difference between point and continuous level?
options: Point level signals at one spot; continuous gives a reading over the whole range
quiz.why: Switches trip at a set point; continuous instruments report the actual level all the time.

quiz.q: A hydrostatic level reading drifts when the product changes. Why?
quiz.why: Hydrostatic level depends on density; a different product changes the pressure per inch of height.

quiz.q: A customer needs a simple high-level alarm to stop a pump. What's a good fit?
options: A point level switch, like a vibrating fork
quiz.why: A point level switch is the simple, low-cost way to trip an alarm or pump at one level.

lessons.title: Valve types, actuators and Cv
lessons.keyPoints:
Ball valves are quarter-turn and give tight shutoff. They're the default for on/off service.
Butterfly valves are quarter-turn, lighter and cheaper in large pipe sizes.
Globe valves move linearly and are the classic choice for throttling (control) service.
Gate valves are for full open or full closed, not throttling.
Check valves stop backflow automatically.
Pneumatic actuators are fast, and spring-return versions fail to a safe position on air loss. Electric actuators fit where there's no instrument air.
A positioner moves a control valve to exactly the position the control signal asks for.
Cv is the flow capacity of a valve: the gallons per minute of water it passes with a 1 psi pressure drop. Size the valve to the needed Cv, not just the pipe size.

quiz.q: A customer needs to throttle flow precisely. Which valve type is the classic choice?
quiz.why: Globe valves are designed for throttling and control.

quiz.q: What does a spring-return pneumatic actuator do if instrument air is lost?
options: Moves the valve to its fail-safe position
quiz.why: The spring drives the valve to its fail-open or fail-closed position.

quiz.q: What does Cv describe?
options: Flow capacity: gpm of water at a 1 psi drop
quiz.why: Cv is the standard measure of how much flow a valve passes.

quiz.q: A large 24" water line needs an economical on/off valve. What's a common choice?
quiz.why: Butterfly valves are lighter and cheaper than other types at large sizes.

lessons.title: Ashcroft: what to lead with
lessons.keyPoints:
Ashcroft is one of the oldest U.S. pressure gauge makers, dating back to the 1850s. Lead with its reputation for heavy-duty process gauges.
The Duragauge (Type 1279) is Ashcroft's flagship process gauge: a solid-front safety design built for tough plant service.
The Type 1009 is a common all-stainless general-purpose gauge for corrosive environments.
Ashcroft's PLUS! performance option dampens vibration and pulsation without liquid fill, so there's no fill to leak or discolor.
The line also covers pressure transmitters, switches, diaphragm seals, test gauges and bimetal thermometers, so you can quote a complete pressure point.
Always confirm current models and options in the latest Ashcroft catalog or PartBuilder before quoting.

quiz.q: Which Ashcroft gauge is its flagship heavy-duty process gauge?
quiz.why: The Duragauge 1279 is Ashcroft's solid-front process gauge for tough service.

quiz.q: What does Ashcroft's PLUS! option do?
options: Dampens vibration and pulsation without liquid fill
Cleans the gauge for oxygen service
quiz.why: PLUS! gives liquid-filled-style dampening with no fill to leak.

quiz.q: A customer needs an all-stainless general-purpose gauge for a corrosive area. Which Ashcroft model fits?
quiz.why: The 1009 is Ashcroft's all-stainless general-purpose gauge.

quiz.q: Before quoting an Ashcroft model, what should you always do?
options: Quote from memory to save time
Confirm the model and options in the current catalog or PartBuilder
Ask the customer for the part number format
quiz.why: Model options change. Checking the current catalog or PartBuilder prevents ordering errors.

lessons.title: WIKA: gauges, transmitters and seals
lessons.keyPoints:
WIKA is a large German family-owned instrumentation maker with a broad pressure and temperature lineup and strong U.S. stocking.
WIKA model numbers describe the gauge family. For example, the 213.53 is a popular liquid-filled brass utility gauge, and the 233.54 is a liquid-filled stainless steel process gauge.
Use the brass utility gauges for air, water and non-corrosive service; step up to the stainless gauges for corrosive media or harsh environments.
WIKA makes pressure transmitters for general industrial use (such as the A-10) and higher-performance applications (such as the S-20).
WIKA is also a major diaphragm seal supplier, so it's a strong fit for corrosive, viscous or sanitary applications that need a seal and gauge or transmitter assembly.
Always confirm current models and options in the latest WIKA catalog or PartBuilder before quoting.

quiz.q: A customer wants an economical liquid-filled gauge for compressed air. Which WIKA model is a typical fit?
quiz.why: Brass utility gauges like the 213.53 suit air, water and other non-corrosive service.

quiz.q: When should you step up from a brass utility gauge to a stainless gauge like the 233.54?
options: When the dial needs to be bigger
When the media or environment is corrosive or harsh
Only when the customer asks for the cheapest option
quiz.why: Stainless wetted parts and cases hold up to corrosive media and harsh plant environments.

quiz.q: Which WIKA product line makes it a strong pick for sanitary or corrosive applications?
quiz.why: WIKA is a major diaphragm seal supplier, so it can build complete seal assemblies.

quiz.q: What's the difference between the WIKA A-10 and S-20 transmitters?
options: The A-10 is for general industrial use; the S-20 is higher performance
quiz.why: The A-10 covers general-purpose needs; the S-20 is the higher-performance option.

lessons.title: Dwyer: low pressure and HVAC
lessons.keyPoints:
Dwyer is known for low-pressure and air-side measurement, with strong ties to HVAC, cleanrooms and building automation. It is now part of DwyerOmega.
The Magnehelic is Dwyer's best-known product: a differential pressure gauge for very low pressures, read in inches of water column.
Typical Magnehelic uses: filter pressure drop, cleanroom room pressure, duct and fan pressure.
The Photohelic adds adjustable switch set points to the same kind of gauge, so it can trigger an alarm or a fan.
Dwyer also offers differential pressure transmitters, air velocity and airflow instruments, and level and flow switches.
When a customer says "inches of water" or "filter monitoring," think Dwyer first. Confirm current models in the latest catalog or PartBuilder before quoting.

quiz.q: What is the Magnehelic used for?
options: Very low differential pressures, like filter drop, in inches of water
quiz.why: The Magnehelic reads very low differential pressures, typically in inches of water column.

quiz.q: What does a Photohelic add compared to a Magnehelic?
options: Adjustable switch set points for alarms or control
quiz.why: The Photohelic includes switches that trip at set points.

quiz.q: A customer says they need to monitor cleanroom pressure in inches of water. Which brand should come to mind first?
quiz.why: Low-pressure, air-side measurement is Dwyer's core strength.

quiz.q: Dwyer is now part of which combined company?
quiz.why: Dwyer combined with Omega under the DwyerOmega name.

lessons.title: How gauge part numbers are built
lessons.keyPoints:
Most gauge part numbers are a code made of segments. Each segment answers one STAMPED-style question.
Common segments: dial size, model or series, wetted materials, connection size and location, options, and range.
Example (Ashcroft style): 45-1279-SS-04L-200# reads as a 4.5-inch dial, Duragauge 1279, stainless steel wetted parts, 1/4-inch NPT lower connection, 0-200 psi.
Options such as liquid fill, oxygen cleaning, special dials or certificates usually add their own codes. Missing one is a common ordering mistake.
Every brand uses its own format, so never translate one brand's code into another's by guessing.
Use PartBuilder or the current catalog to build the exact number, then read it back to the customer in plain words before you order.

quiz.q: In the Ashcroft-style number 45-1279-SS-04L-200#, what does "04L" mean?
quiz.why: 04L is the connection: 1/4-inch NPT, lower (bottom) mount.

quiz.q: In the same number, what does "45" stand for?
quiz.why: The leading segment is the dial size, 4.5 inches.

quiz.q: What's a common way part-number orders go wrong?
options: Leaving out an option code like liquid fill or oxygen cleaning
quiz.why: Options carry their own codes. Skip one and the customer gets the wrong gauge.

quiz.q: What's the best last step before placing the order?
options: Guess the code from another brand
Read the part number back to the customer in plain words
quiz.why: Reading it back in plain words catches mistakes before they ship.

scenarios.title: Shaking gauge at the pump
scenarios.persona: Mike, maintenance tech at a city water treatment plant
scenarios.opening: Hey, I've got pressure gauges on our high-service pump discharge that keep dying every few months. The needle shakes so bad you can't even read it. What have you got?
scenarios.hidden: Normal pressure is about 85 psi, with spikes when the pump starts. Current gauges are 2.5-inch dry brass, 0-100 psi. Mounted right on the pump discharge, outdoors. 1/4-inch NPT bottom connection. Needs 6 of them within a week.
scenarios.goodRec: A liquid-filled stainless steel gauge with a larger dial (4 or 4.5 inch), range around 0-160 or 0-200 psi so 85 psi sits near mid-scale, plus a snubber to handle the start-up spikes.

scenarios.title: Sanitary pressure on a dairy line
scenarios.persona: Karen, process engineer at a dairy
scenarios.opening: Hi, I need pressure readings on our pasteurizer line. The old gauge got flagged in an audit and I need something that'll pass.
scenarios.hidden: 1.5-inch tri-clamp connections. Normal 30 psi, max 60 psi. CIP cleaning with hot caustic around 180 F. 3-A sanitary required. Would like a 4-20 mA signal to the PLC eventually. Food-grade fill if any fill fluid is used.
scenarios.goodRec: A sanitary 3-A diaphragm seal with tri-clamp connection and food-grade fill, on a gauge or a sanitary pressure transmitter with 4-20 mA. Range around 0-60 or 0-100 psi.

scenarios.title: Steam flow for cost allocation
scenarios.persona: Raj, utilities engineer at a chemical plant
scenarios.opening: I need to start measuring the steam going to one of our process units so we can charge it back to them. The old orifice plate on that line is shot.
scenarios.hidden: 4-inch line. Saturated steam at about 150 psig. Flow from 2,000 to 10,000 lb per hour. DCS takes 4-20 mA with HART. Would prefer less permanent pressure loss than the orifice.
scenarios.goodRec: A vortex flowmeter, ideally with built-in pressure or temperature compensation to output mass flow, or a multivariable DP setup. Confirm the turndown covers 2,000 to 10,000 lb/hr.

scenarios.title: Tank level with foam
scenarios.persona: Dana, operations lead at a chemical blending plant
scenarios.opening: Our level transmitter on one of the mixing tanks goes crazy every time the agitator kicks on. I need something that actually works.
scenarios.hidden: Current unit is ultrasonic. 12-foot tank. Heavy foam and solvent vapor when mixing. Class I Division 2 area. Needs 4-20 mA. Also wants a separate high-level alarm because they overflowed once.
scenarios.goodRec: Guided wave radar (or high-frequency non-contact radar) with the right hazardous-area approval, plus an independent point level switch such as a vibrating fork for the high-level alarm.

scenarios.title: Sour gas compressor gauges
scenarios.persona: Travis, field supervisor at a natural gas compressor station
scenarios.opening: I need to replace a bunch of pressure gauges on our compressor lines. Can you quote me something?
scenarios.hidden: Gas contains H2S, so NACE MR0175 materials are required. Normal pressure about 1,200 psi. Strong vibration from the compressors. Outdoors in heat and cold. Company requires safety-pattern gauges (solid front, blowout back) above 1,000 psi.
scenarios.goodRec: NACE-compliant wetted parts (stainless or Monel), liquid-filled safety-pattern gauge, range about 0-2,000 or 0-3,000 psi, plus a snubber.

scenarios.title: Oxygen service gauges
scenarios.persona: Angela, purchasing agent at an industrial gas filling plant
scenarios.opening: I need gauges for our oxygen cylinder filling station. Our last supplier shipped the wrong ones and I can't have that again.
scenarios.hidden: Cylinders fill to about 2,200 psi. Gauges must be cleaned for oxygen service and marked 'Use No Oil'. Needs cleaning certification paperwork. Quantity 20.
scenarios.goodRec: Gauges cleaned and certified for oxygen service, marked 'Use No Oil', safety-pattern construction, range around 0-4,000 psi, with cleaning certification included.

specs.title: Batching vegetable oil
specs.application: A food plant wants to batch vegetable oil accurately into mixing tanks. 2-inch stainless line, room temperature, about 20 gpm. They want high accuracy and a 4-20 mA output to the batch controller.
specs.why: Oil isn't conductive, so a mag meter won't work. Coriolis measures mass directly with high accuracy, which is ideal for batching.

specs.title: Cleanroom filter monitoring
specs.application: A pharma plant needs a local gauge showing pressure drop across HVAC filters for a cleanroom. The drop runs from about 0.2 to 0.8 inches of water column. No signal needed, just a reading for the daily walk-through.
options: Low-range differential pressure gauge, such as a Dwyer Magnehelic, 0-1 in. w.c.
specs.why: Filter loading is a very low differential pressure in inches of water. A low-range DP gauge like the Magnehelic is built for exactly this.

specs.title: Furnace temperature at 1,800 F
specs.application: A heat-treating furnace runs at about 1,800 F (around 980 C). The customer needs a temperature signal to the controller and wants the sensor to be replaceable without shutting down.
options: Pt100 RTD in the open air
Thermocouple in a protection tube or thermowell
specs.why: At 1,800 F you're past the range of standard RTDs. A thermocouple in a protective well handles the heat and can be replaced without shutdown.

specs.title: Abrasive slurry pump discharge
specs.application: A plant pumps a thick, abrasive slurry. Standard gauges plug up within weeks and the readings freeze. Pressure is about 60 psi. They need a local reading.
options: Standard brass gauge with a snubber
Gauge with a diaphragm seal, such as an inline (flow-through) seal
specs.why: Solids clog the gauge socket. A diaphragm seal keeps the slurry out of the gauge, and an inline seal is self-cleaning in the flow.

specs.title: Throttling cooling water
specs.application: A customer wants to automatically control cooling water flow to a heat exchanger to hold a process temperature. The plant has instrument air and the DCS outputs 4-20 mA.
options: Globe control valve with a pneumatic actuator and positioner
Ball valve with a manual lever
specs.why: Precise throttling calls for a globe control valve. Pneumatic actuation uses their instrument air, and the positioner follows the 4-20 mA signal.

specs.title: Temporary flow check without shutdown
specs.application: A wastewater plant wants to check pump flow on a 10-inch line for a few weeks to settle a performance dispute. The line can't be shut down or cut.
specs.why: Clamp-on ultrasonic straps onto the outside of the pipe, so no cutting or shutdown is needed. It's ideal for temporary checks.
